strengths: The central idea is simple but well-motivated and clearly articulated: decouple visual localization (IRD) from reasoning via a two-stage prompting pipeline, enabling perception-only test-time scaling and asymmetric compute allocation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: four models across two families (Qwen3-VL 4B/8B, Molmo2 4B/8B), three input resolutions, three high-fidelity perception benchmarks (V*, HRBench-4k/8k), plus a genuinely OOD remote-sensing suite (XLRS), with expanded tables, prompts, and hyperparameters in the appendix.

The paper reports a useful set of findings beyond the headline numbers: the oracle-crop 'resolution compensation' analysis (Figures 2, 4, A.1, A.2), the observation that low-resolution SFT acts as a regularizer and outperforms full-resolution training, and the crop-expansion ablation showing tight bounding boxes are not always optimal.

The perception-only self-consistency via Weighted Boxes Fusion is a sensible and efficient alternative to ensembling full reasoning chains, with the crop-count analysis (Table 9) supporting the claimed efficiency argument.

Strong headline results: training-free gains over native and 'thinking with images' baselines, and with SFT the 8B model surpasses much larger and RL-trained competitors on V* (Table 5), supporting the claim that perception is the bottleneck.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported: exact prompts, LoRA hyperparameters, training compute, decoding protocol (greedy), and synthetic data-generation procedure are documented.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially a two-step prompting scheme (ask for relevant crops, then re-prompt with crops), which is close to existing visual-prompting and crop-then-reason approaches; the paper itself concedes it is 'an effective prompting scheme'. The neuroscientific framing (What/Where pathways, prefrontal cortex) is decorative and does not inform any design decision or analysis.

Evaluation is restricted to multiple-choice benchmarks with greedy decoding; there are no open-ended VQA or downstream task evaluations, and no statistical significance testing, error bars, or multiple seeds, despite small benchmarks like V* (~190 images), where differences of a few points may not be meaningful.

Baseline comparability is imperfect: the authors acknowledge reproduction issues with the 'thinking with images' baseline on Qwen3-VL, and several baseline cells are missing in Table 1 (e.g., Molmo2 'Thinking w/ images' at 512/Full in both ID and OOD), weakening the completeness of the head-to-head comparison.

The SFT data is generated by Qwen3-VL-235B using its own 'thinking with images' traces with rejection sampling on correct answers; comparing this distilled 8B model against the 235B teacher as a baseline (Table 5) raises questions about distillation-driven gains and possible benchmark-specific supervision, which the paper does not fully dissect.

The efficiency claims are not rigorously quantified: the '200x lower token budget' and the Pareto-front analysis (Figure 3) rely on an efficiency axis whose accounting (rollout counts, crop sizes, shared KV-cache savings) is not precisely specified, and the latency benefit of two sequential calls versus a single interleaved chain is asserted rather than measured.

Some claims are under-supported: 'without forgetting the model's generic capabilities' (Section 1) is claimed but never tested with general-purpose benchmarks; the counter-intuitive low-resolution-training result, while interesting, is explained post hoc with plausible-sounding hypotheses rather than validated mechanistically.

Method generality is untested for queries requiring multiple hops or global context (the paper's own A.2 analysis shows enlarged crops can help), and there is no analysis of failure cases for SPARC itself analogous to the qualitative failure analysis provided for the baseline.

strengths: The motivating analysis (Section 3, Figure 2) is a clean and informative controlled experiment showing how crop localization accuracy trades off against image resolution, and it reasonably justifies the proposed two-stage design.

The empirical evaluation is broad for this type of work: two model families (Qwen3-VL, Molmo2), two model sizes, three in-domain benchmarks (V*, HRBench-4K/8K) plus an OOD remote-sensing suite, with expanded per-benchmark tables in the appendix.

The paper identifies a genuinely useful practical regime: in low-resolution settings, cropping recovers high-frequency detail lost to downsizing (e.g., XLRS at 256px with ~0.1% of visual tokens), and the Pareto-frontier analysis quantifies the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
The method is simple and largely reproducible: the full IRD and QA prompts, LoRA hyperparameters, training setup, and WBF parameters (IoU threshold, temperature) are provided in the appendix.

The asymmetric self-consistency idea (Section 5) — ensembling only the cheap coordinate-generation step and fusing with WBF rather than running N full reasoning chains — is a sensible and well-motivated efficiency mechanism, supported by crop-count measurements (Table 9).
weaknesses: Limited originality. The core contribution — localize relevant regions first, then answer conditioned on high-resolution crops — is close to existing training-free approaches the paper itself cites (Wang et al. 2024 'divide, conquer and combine', Zhang et al. 2025 'MLLMs know where to look', and the V* guided-search line). The added elements (WBF fusion of crop rollouts, LoRA SFT on the detection step) are incremental engineering rather than a new understanding or method.

The neuroscience framing is decorative and unsupported. Calling the stages 'What/Where Circuits' and a 'Prefrontal Cortex Circuit' suggests a biologically grounded architecture, but no experiment tests any claim connecting the pipeline to the cited neuroscience; the method is standard two-step prompting. The framing overstates the contribution's conceptual depth.

Concerns about the main baseline weaken the central claims. The authors admit 'reproducibility issues' with Qwen3-VL 'thinking with images' and report cases where it underperforms the native model (e.g., 36.8 vs 41.7 at 256px; 48.3 vs 53.5 OOD full). Since 'thinking with images' is the primary competitor, an apparently miscalibrated baseline makes the headline gains (e.g., +6.7 points on V*, +4.6 OOD) hard to trust at face value.

Gains at full resolution — the setting where comparisons are most meaningful — are small and within plausible noise (Qwen3VL-4B: 74.8 vs 73.1 vs 72.6; Qwen3VL-8B: 79.5 vs 78.1 vs 79.0), yet no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported anywhere, despite the claim of 'consistent performance gains across all benchmarks'.

The 'no forgetting / independent optimization' claim (Section 1, Section 6) is asserted but not verified: all evaluations are on perception-centric multiple-choice benchmarks; no experiment shows the reasoning model's general (non-perceptual) capabilities are preserved after SFT.

Internal inconsistencies suggest insufficient polish: Section 5.2 refers to 'Qwen2VL 4B' where Qwen3VL-4B is meant; Table 5 in the appendix carries a typo ('Performance of out proposed'); the Table 1 caption says OOD is XLRS while the OOD 'Full' column for Molmo2-8B (39.0) is below native (39.1), contradicting the text's uniform-improvement narrative.

Evaluation is restricted to multiple-choice VQA benchmarks where cropping is known to help; generalization to open-ended VQA, documents, or other perceptual tasks is untested. The synthetic SFT data (~23K/14K samples via teacher-model rejection sampling) is described only briefly and no code or data release is mentioned.

The limitations discussion is essentially absent (a one-sentence impact statement and scattered acknowledgments of baseline reproducibility and Molmo2-4B distillation plateau), leaving material caveats — such as dependence on strong native grounding ability and the ill-posedness of the 'optimal crop' — underexplored in the main text.

strengths: The core idea is simple and practical: decoupling perception (implicit relevance detection producing crops) from reasoning via structured two-stage prompting, enabling training-free gains across four models (Qwen3-VL-4B/8B, Molmo2-4B/8B) and multiple benchmarks, including an OOD remote-sensing suite.

The asymmetric test-time scaling insight is genuinely useful: self-consistency applied only to the lightweight perception stage (with Weighted Boxes Fusion) improves accuracy without the linear cost of full-chain ensembling, and the crop-count analysis (Table 9) supports the efficiency claims.

The empirical study is thorough: controlled crop-overlap ablations (Figures 2, 4), crop-expansion analysis showing IRD is ill-posed (Figure 5, A.2), Pareto-frontier efficiency analysis (Figure 3), and an interesting counter-intuitive finding that low-resolution SFT training acts as a regularizer and outperforms full-resolution distillation (Table 3).

Reproducibility artifacts are relatively strong: full prompts, hyperparameters (Table 4), training details, and expanded result tables (Tables 7-9) are provided, and honest discussion of reproduction issues with the 'thinking with images' baseline is given.
The distinction of IRD from standard REC (optimal crop ≠ tightest bounding box) is a useful conceptual framing backed by the crop-expansion ablation.
weaknesses: Novelty is modest: the pipeline is essentially 'detect relevant crops, then re-prompt with them', which is closely related to existing visual-search and zoom-in approaches (e.g., training-free crop prompting, Visual Sketchpad, prior V* derivative work). The neuroscience motivation (what/where pathways, prefrontal cortex) is largely decorative and does not translate into any technical commitment that could be validated or falsified.

Benchmarks are narrow and all primarily perceptual multiple-choice tasks (V*, HRBench-4K/8K, XLRS). The claim of general 'test-time scaling of VLMs' is not supported by standard general VQA/reasoning suites (e.g., MMMU, MathVista, general VQA), so the scope of the contribution is narrower than the framing suggests. The OOD claim rests on a single remote-sensing benchmark.

The headline '200x lower token budget' and the efficiency analysis (Figure 3) lack a transparent token accounting; the x-axis definition and how KV-cache sharing and rollout overhead are counted are not clearly specified, making the efficiency claims hard to verify.

Baselines were largely reproduced by the authors (marked with *), and the reproduced 'thinking with images' results sometimes fall below native performance, raising concerns about baseline fairness; no external numbers under identical settings are available for Molmo2. No variance, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported anywhere, despite sampling-based components (T=0.7 rollouts) in the pipeline.

The SFT experiments introduce potential contamination ambiguity: synthetic annotations are generated by rejection sampling on traces that 'yield a correct final answer' (Section 6.1) using a 235B teacher; the paper does not clarify whether this filtering used the evaluation tasks themselves, which would inflate the w/ SFT results (e.g., 91.2% on V*).

Several presentation inconsistencies undermine polish: 'Qwen2VL 4B' typo in Section 5.2, missing cells in Table 1 (Molmo2 512 'thinking with images'), text stating SFT for two epochs while Table 4 reports five, and some discrepancies between abstract claims and table values. No code release is mentioned.

Single-shot cropping without iterative refinement limits the method to tasks where one localization suffices; failure cases where reasoning should guide further search (the iterative zoom-in cycles deferred to future work) are precisely where 'thinking with images' may retain an advantage, and the paper does not quantify when SPARC loses.

strengths: Comprehensive and multi-faceted evaluation: the method is tested across two model families (Qwen3-VL 4B/8B/235B-A22B and Molmo2 4B/8B), three perception-heavy benchmarks (V*, HRBench-4K/8K), an OOD remote-sensing suite (XLRS), and a general benchmark (MME-Realworld) to check for regressions — a breadth that goes well beyond typical 'one benchmark' papers.

The paper supports its central design decisions empirically rather than just asserting them: the crop-overlap ablation (Figure 2, Appendix A.1) justifies the low-resolution + accurate-crop premise; Appendix A.2 characterizes the ill-posedness of the crop task; Appendix A.5 honestly compares against a bottom-up divide-and-conquer variant, showing SPARC's efficiency advantage (e.g., ~1.9 vs ~11 crops) rather than hiding the cases where bottom-up wins at low resolution.

The asymmetric self-consistency idea (WBF over perception rollouts with KV-cache sharing) is a genuinely nice, practical contribution: Table 6 shows the perception stage converges on near-perfect intersection with ground truth while deduplicating 85 crops down to ~2.4, and the crop-count analysis gives a mechanistic account of why consensus improves with resolution.

The modular SFT result (training a LoRA only on the perception step, outperforming full-resolution distillation when trained at low resolution, and beating an end-to-end distillation SFT baseline in Appendix A.10) supports the decoupled-training claim with a real control, and the low-resolution training effect is a useful, counter-intuitive finding.

Practical relevance: latency measurements (TTFT/E2E, Table 8) and the 0.1% visual token claim on 8500x8500 XLRS images demonstrate real-world efficiency, not just token counts; prompts, hyperparameters, and decoding parameters are disclosed, aiding reproducibility.

Clear writing, with honest reporting of failure modes (e.g., Molmo2-8B SFT plateau attributed to weak teacher, 'thinking with images' instability on Qwen3-VL) and an explicit limitations paragraph on reliance on native grounding.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core mechanism is a two-step 'localize then answer' prompting pipeline plus bounding-box fusion over rollouts. Closely related training-free zoom/crop approaches (e.g., Zhang et al. 2025a 'MLLMs know where to look', divide-and-conquer high-resolution methods, V*'s visual search) already implement variants of this; the paper's framing (neuroscience 'circuits', context engineering) is heavier than the actual technical delta, which is largely careful engineering.

Baseline fairness concerns: the 'thinking with images' comparison uses off-the-shelf generation parameters and the authors admit instability ('sometimes does not even reach the native model performance', with TwI underperforming native at 256/512 in several Table 14 rows). Headline claims (e.g., 'surpassing thinking with images by 4.6 points in an OOD setting with a 200x lower token budget') are hard to reconstruct precisely from the reported tables, and gains over the native baseline alone at full resolution are modest in some cells (e.g., Molmo2-8B OOD Full: 39.1 native vs 39.0 SPARC).

No statistical significance or variance reporting: results are single-run with greedy decoding on relatively small subsets (e.g., 16 QA pairs for V* Far Objects in A.7; small filtered GQA subset); for several comparisons the margins are 1-2 points, where sampling variance and prompt sensitivity could matter. No confidence intervals or repeated-seed evidence are provided.

Mixed results are not always foregrounded: in Table 12 (MME-Realworld), Qwen3-VL 8B SPARC underperforms native at 256 (26.1 vs 28.7) and slightly at Full on several reasoning splits, yet the text concludes SPARC 'maintains, and frequently improves, performance'. A more balanced characterization would strengthen the paper.

The neuroscience motivation is largely decorative: nothing in the method or experiments tests the 'separate what/where/pre-frontal circuits' claim beyond analogy, so the framing risks overstating the mechanistic insight.

No explicit code or data release statement; combined with dependence on specific native-grounding model behaviors (JSON/point output formats) and an undisclosed 'official' TwI implementation, independent reproduction of the exact comparisons is not guaranteed.

Some claims require SFT to hold at the advertised magnitude: the 6.7-point improvement on V* (Table 14) requires the SFT 256 variant, not the training-free SPARC the abstract's framing might suggest; the zero-shot gain at full resolution is smaller (+1.6).

strengths: The core empirical finding is convincing and useful: a simple two-stage prompt (localize first, then reason over crops) improves VLM perception-heavy QA in a fully training-free manner, and the paper demonstrates this consistently across two model families (Qwen3-VL, Molmo2), multiple sizes (4B–235B), three token budgets, and four benchmarks (V*, HRBench-4K/8K, XLRS as OOD).

The controlled crop-perturbation experiment (Figure 2, Figure 4) is a nice diagnostic that motivates the method quantitatively: it shows accurate low-resolution crops recover full-resolution performance, establishing the efficiency trade-off the method exploits.

The asymmetric test-time scaling idea (WBF aggregation over cheap IRD rollouts instead of expensive full-chain ensembling) is a sensible and well-executed efficiency contribution, with a supporting ablation up to 64 rollouts (Table 6) showing saturation and compression behavior.

The appendix is unusually thorough: bottom-up divide-and-conquer comparison (A.5), latency measurements (A.8), distilled-SFT baseline showing catastrophic forgetting (A.10), larger-model scaling (A.11), general-capability checks on MME RealWorld (A.12), qualitative failure cases, and hyperparameters—this supports reproducibility and honest self-assessment.
The paper is candid about unstable 'thinking with images' baselines and about the Molmo2-4B distillation bottleneck failure case.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to prior work. The central mechanism—training-free localization of relevant regions followed by re-answering over high-resolution crops—is closely related to already-published approaches the paper itself cites (Zhang et al., 2025a 'MLLMs know where to look'; Wang et al., 2025b 'Divide, conquer and combine'; V* visual search). The neuroscience framing (what/where pathways, prefrontal cortex) is largely decorative and does not generate testable predictions or shape the method. What remains genuinely new is the WBF-over-IRD-rollouts aggregation and the decoupled LoRA fine-tuning, which are incremental.

Data contamination is not addressed. Training data for the perception LoRA is generated by rejection sampling on the DeepEyes dataset, and evaluation is on V* and HRBench—the paper never discusses whether these sets overlap with the SFT corpus. Given the rejection-sampling filter explicitly selects traces that yield correct answers on the source data, this omission must be resolved before the SFT gains (Section 6, Table 4) can be trusted.

Evidential rigor is thin for the margin of many claims. All results use greedy decoding with single runs and no confidence intervals or significance testing; several reported margins are small (e.g., Qwen3-VL 8B full-resolution gains of 0.5–1.7 points; GQA Global subset differences of 2–3 points on only 157 QA pairs; WBF ablation accuracy fluctuating 88.0–89.5 non-monotonically). Without variance estimates it is unclear which cell-level improvements are real, and the comparison against an unstable 'thinking with images' baseline (which sometimes underperforms the native model) further muddies the headline comparisons.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the tables. In Table 5 the 'Bottom-up SPARC' rows for Molmo2 4B and Molmo2 8B are identical in both accuracy and crop counts (62.3/64.7/69.3 and 11.60/11.05/9.84)—almost certainly a copy-paste error. Table 4 claims 'systematic performance improvements' with 'the sole exception Molmo2-4B', yet Molmo2-8B SFT gains are within noise (59.1→59.6 average full-res) and several SFT cells underperform the zero-shot SPARC baseline.

The claimed 'circuit' interpretation (Figure 1) overreaches: sequential prompting activates two output distributions of the same frozen model; there is no evidence of distinct functional circuits, and the paper's own attribution to 'context engineering principles' is the more parsimonious explanation.

Robustness of the method to prompt phrasing is unexamined. The authors state that enforcing strict JSON/point output format was 'the single most critical factor for ensuring robust instruction adherence', which suggests fragility, yet no prompt-variation sensitivity analysis is provided.

The abstract's strongest claims (200× lower token budget, 0.1% of visual tokens on XLRS) are efficiency statements computed against full-resolution baselines that are known to be dominated by token count; the more meaningful Pareto comparison (Figure 3) supports a real but more modest advantage, and Table 8's 200× TTFT figure compares SPARC-256 against TwI-full where TwI is already slower even than SPARC-full.

strengths: The paper is well-structured and empirically thorough: it evaluates across two model families (Qwen3-VL, Molmo2), multiple model scales (4B, 8B, 235B-A22B), three input resolutions, and four benchmarks (V*, HRBench-4K/8K, XLRS as OOD), which gives the central claims reasonable breadth of support.

The motivating analysis (Figure 2, Appendix A.1) is a genuinely useful diagnostic: showing that accurate crop localization at low resolution can match full-resolution performance establishes the paper's premise (perception can be offloaded to a separate, cheap localization step) with controlled evidence rather than assertion.

The asymmetric test-time scaling idea is well executed: applying self-consistency only to the lightweight coordinate-generation step and fusing via WBF achieves accuracy gains (up to ~10 points at low resolution) with sublinear crop growth, and the WBF diagnostics in Appendix A.6 (union area, coverage loss, scaling to 64 rollouts) are careful and transparent.

The decoupled SFT experiments are a solid contribution: the finding that low-resolution training acts as a regularizer and outperforms full-resolution distillation is counter-intuitive and well supported, and the Distillation SFT baseline (Appendix A.10) demonstrates the catastrophic-forgetting risk of entangled training that SPARC avoids.

The paper is honest about weaknesses: unstable 'thinking with images' behavior, the Molmo2-4B distillation bottleneck, Molmo2-8B underperformance, brittle latency metrics, and the reliance on models with native grounding are all acknowledged rather than hidden.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: prompts are provided in full (A.3), hyperparameters in detail (A.9), and baseline generation parameters are specified (A.13).
weaknesses: Originality is modest at its core: the method is a two-step prompt (localize, then re-prompt with crops), which is close to prior training-free work such as Zhang et al. (2025a) 'MLLMs know where to look' and divide-and-conquer high-resolution pipelines. The claimed novelty rests mainly on framing (neuroscience-inspired 'circuits'), WBF-based perceptual consistency, and decoupled SFT — incremental advances over existing zoom-in approaches.

The neuroscience motivation ('What and Where Circuits', 'Prefrontal Cortex Circuit') is largely decorative: the method is prompt sequencing over the same VLM, with no analysis linking model behavior to the claimed biological separation. This framing risks overstating what the contribution actually is.

There are data-integrity and reporting red flags: Table 5 contains verbatim identical rows for Molmo2 4B and Molmo2 8B bottom-up variants (62.3/64.7/69.3 and 11.60/11.05/9.84), which is almost certainly a copy-paste error and undermines confidence in the tables; and the abstract's headline numbers ('6.7 points on V*', '4.6 points OOD with 200x lower token budget') are difficult to trace to any single table in the manuscript.

Statistical rigor is thin: results are greedy-decoded single runs without error bars or significance tests, and several margins are small. Some probe sets are very small (V* Far Objects has only 16 QA pairs), making those robustness claims weak.

Potential train/test contamination is not discussed: SFT data is generated via rejection sampling on the DeepEyes dataset, and the relationship of that data to the evaluation benchmarks (especially V*) is not analyzed, which matters for the SFT claims.

The 'thinking with images' baseline is unstable (sometimes below native performance), which complicates the central comparison — the paper acknowledges this but does not fully resolve whether SPARC's advantage over the paradigm reflects method superiority or baseline misconfiguration.

The GQA Global results (19-27% accuracy for both methods) are very low and unexplained, and Table 13 is mislabeled as a table despite being a figure; these suggest insufficient polish in the evaluation and presentation.
